title: Count the Evens
concept: Looping over a list and counting matches
brief: Counts how many numbers in the list are even.
description: Walk through the list of whole numbers and count how many of them are even (divisible by 2 with no remainder). Negative numbers can be even too, so -4 counts just like 4 does.
solution:
def count_evens(nums):
    return len([n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
hints: Use the % operator to check if a number leaves a remainder when divided by 2.
You can build a small list of just the even numbers and then check its length, or keep a running counter as you loop.
explainer: The solution loops through every number and keeps the ones where n % 2 equals 0, since that's the test for being even, then counts how many survived.

title: Biggest Gap
brief: Finds the gap between the largest and smallest number in the list.
description: Given a list with at least one number, figure out the biggest number and the smallest number, then return how far apart they are. If every number is the same, the gap is 0.
hints: Python has built-in max() and min() functions that work directly on a list.
The answer is just the biggest value minus the smallest value.
explainer: max(nums) finds the largest value and min(nums) finds the smallest, so subtracting one from the other gives the total spread of the list.

title: Centered Average
concept: Combining sum(), max(), and min() to build a custom average
brief: Averages a list after setting aside one copy of the highest and lowest value.
description: Given a list of at least 3 numbers, imagine removing one copy of the largest value and one copy of the smallest value, then return the average of whatever numbers are left. The answer can come out as a decimal.
hints: You don't have to physically remove anything from the list -- just subtract one max and one min from the total sum.
Divide by how many numbers are left over, which is the original length minus 2.
explainer: Subtracting one max and one min from the total sum leaves exactly the sum of the 'middle' numbers, and dividing that by (length - 2) gives their average.

title: Sum but Skip the 13s
concept: Looping with a 'skip the next item' flag
brief: Adds up a list of numbers, but a 13 and whatever comes right after it don't count.
description: Add up all the numbers in the list, except whenever you hit a 13, skip it completely and also skip the very next number after it, no matter what it is. Then keep adding normally from there.
hints: Keep a True/False flag that remembers 'the last thing I saw was a 13, so ignore the next value.'
When you see a 13, don't add it -- just turn the skip flag on and move to the next number.
explainer: A flag named skip tracks whether the current number should be ignored because it followed a 13; seeing a 13 turns the flag on instead of adding to the total, and the flag is cleared right after skipping one number.

title: Sum but Skip 6-to-7
brief: Adds up a list of numbers, but ignores everything from a 6 up through the next 7.
description: Add up all the numbers in the list, but whenever you see a 6, stop adding numbers until you see a 7 -- and don't count the 6 or the 7 either. After that 7 shows up, go back to adding normally.
hints: Keep a True/False flag for 'am I currently inside a 6...7 stretch?'
While the flag is on, the only thing that matters is watching for the 7 that turns it back off.
explainer: A skipping flag turns on at a 6 and only turns back off once a 7 is seen, so every value in between (including the 6 and 7 themselves) is skipped instead of added.

title: Adjacent Twos
concept: Checking neighboring pairs in a list
brief: Checks whether two 2s ever sit right next to each other in the list.
description: Look through the list for a spot where one 2 is immediately followed by another 2. Return True if that ever happens, and False if it never does.
hints: Loop using an index so you can look at nums[i] and nums[i+1] at the same time.
Stop as soon as you find one matching pair -- you don't need to check the whole list after that.
explainer: The loop compares each number to the one right after it, and returns True the moment both of them are 2; if the loop finishes without finding that, the answer is False.

title: Unlucky Number
brief: Checks that the number 13 never shows up anywhere in the list.
description: Some drone pilots consider 13 an unlucky reading, so this function checks a list of numbers and returns True only if 13 never appears in it at all. If 13 shows up even once, return False.
solution:
def lucky13(nums):
    return 13 not in nums
hints: Python's `in` keyword can check whether a value exists anywhere inside a list.
You want the opposite of 'is 13 in the list', so think about the `not` keyword.
explainer: The `in` operator scans the whole list for a matching value, and `not` flips that result so the function reports True exactly when no 13 was found.

title: Sum but Skip the 28s
concept: Looping with a 'skip the next item' flag
brief: Adds up a list of numbers, but a 28 and whatever comes right after it don't count.
description: Add up all the numbers in the list, except whenever you hit a 28, skip it completely and also skip the very next number after it, no matter what it is. Then keep adding normally from there.
hints: This works just like skipping after a 13, except the trigger number is 28 instead.
Keep a True/False flag that remembers 'the last thing I saw was a 28, so ignore the next value.'
explainer: A flag named skip tracks whether the current number should be ignored because it followed a 28; seeing a 28 turns the flag on instead of adding to the total, and the flag is cleared right after skipping one number.

title: More Ones Than Fours
brief: Checks whether the number 1 appears more often than the number 4 in the list.
description: Count how many times 1 shows up in the list and how many times 4 shows up. Return True only if 1 shows up strictly more often than 4 does.
hints: Lists have a built-in .count(value) method that tells you how many times a value appears.
Compare the two counts directly with a greater-than sign.
explainer: nums.count(1) and nums.count(4) each tally up how many times that number appears, and the function just compares those two totals.

title: Only Ones and Fours
concept: Checking that every item in a list matches a condition
brief: Checks that every number in the list is either a 1 or a 4.
description: Look at every number in the list. If every single one of them is either 1 or 4, return True. If even one number is something else, return False. An empty list counts as True since there's nothing to break the rule.
hints: You can loop through the list and return False the moment you find a number that isn't 1 or 4.
If the loop finishes without ever returning False, that means every number passed the test.
explainer: The loop checks each number, and any value that is not 1 and not 4 immediately fails the test; surviving the whole loop means the list only ever contained 1s and 4s.

title: No One-Four in a Row
concept: Checking neighboring pairs in a list
brief: Checks that a 1 is never immediately followed by a 4 in the list.
description: Look through the list for a spot where a 1 is immediately followed by a 4. Return False if that ever happens, and True if it never does.
hints: Loop using an index so you can compare nums[i] with nums[i+1].
The moment you spot a 1 directly followed by a 4, you already know the answer is False.
explainer: The loop checks every pair of neighbors, and returns False as soon as it finds a 1 sitting right before a 4; otherwise it returns True once it has checked them all.

title: Value Is Everywhere
concept: Checking that every neighboring pair satisfies a condition
brief: Checks that a chosen value shows up in every pair of neighboring elements in the list.
description: Given a list and a target value, look at every pair of numbers that sit next to each other. Return True only if the target value appears in each and every one of those neighboring pairs. A list with 0 or 1 numbers has no pairs to fail, so it's automatically True.
hints: Walk through the list comparing each neighboring pair, nums[i] and nums[i+1].
A pair only fails the test if NEITHER of its two numbers equals val.
explainer: Each neighboring pair is checked, and the function bails out with False the instant it finds a pair where neither number matches val; making it through every pair means val truly is everywhere.
